label: Chapter 6: Leopold's Capital, the Belle Époque and the Congo, 1831 to 1914

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The new Belgium turned out to be a remarkable success story.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Didn't it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Brussels is its showcase. Belgium is the first country on the European continent to undergo an industrial revolution, following the example of Britain.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Coal and iron in the south, textiles in Flanders, and a good banking system.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Real wealth.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the railways.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1835, the first railway on the continent opens, between Brussels and the nearby city of Mechelen.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And within a few years, the country has a dense network of tracks, with Brussels at the center.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The population grows fast, and the capital swells with civil servants, bankers, merchants, and workers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It also became a refuge for ideas.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1834, liberal Brussels founds a new university, the Free University of Brussels, dedicated to free inquiry, independent of both state and church.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And because the new Belgian constitution is so liberal, the city attracts writers, thinkers, and political refugees from across Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Baudelaire, Victor Hugo.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Charles Baudelaire stayed there.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Victor Hugo lived for a time on the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1873, in a Brussels hotel room, the poet Paul Verlaine shot and wounded his young lover, the poet Arthur Rimbaud.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then went to jail in Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, that is dramatic. I was not expecting that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Poets. What can you do.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But one exile, above all, left a mark.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1845, the young German philosopher Karl Marx, expelled from France, comes to Brussels with his wife and family, and he stays until 1848.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With his friend Friedrich Engels, he writes a pamphlet in Brussels, in the winter of 1847 and 1848, called the Manifesto of the Communist Party.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Published elsewhere, though.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In London, in February of 1848.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Marx is expelled from Belgium a few weeks later.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The pamphlet went on to shape the history of the twentieth century.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that's one very productive winter.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Well, he did get thrown out.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Meanwhile, the river had become a problem.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A disaster. The Senne, which made Brussels possible, runs through the middle of the city, an open sewer, choked with refuse, and it floods regularly.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It carries cholera. And the stench in summer is notorious.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So they buried it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the eighteen-sixties, the city's reforming mayor, Jules Anspach, decides to bury it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Between 1867 and 1871, the river is covered with a long brick vault.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And above it, the city builds a grand new avenue lined with elegant buildings, modeled on the Paris boulevards of Baron Haussmann.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Boulevard Anspach.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Named after the mayor who built it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The river is still there today, flowing in a tunnel beneath the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They also build a stock exchange, the Bourse, in the heart of the new district, and the whole center is transformed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So that's the river I said sounded impossible in the Welcome.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the river. See? We got there.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: We got there. It sounds like a triumph.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was an enormous achievement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And also a loss. Hundreds of old houses and streets in the working-class neighborhoods were torn down, and whole communities were uprooted.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there was another giant project, the Palace of Justice.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1866, work begins on a vast new Palace of Justice, designed by the architect Joseph Poelaert, on a hill above the Marolles.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When it's finished in 1883, it's often described as the largest building constructed anywhere in the nineteenth century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A colossal mass of columns, domes, and staircases that dwarfs the city around it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I bet the neighbors weren't thrilled.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To build it, the authorities flattened part of the old working-class Marolles district.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Locals have grumbled about it ever since.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Fair enough. Now, we get to Leopold the Second.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1865, Leopold the First dies, and his son takes the throne as Leopold the Second.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He reigns for forty-four years, and he's ambitious in a way his father wasn't.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He feels his country is too small, and he dreams of an empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The great European powers are carving up Africa, and Leopold wants a piece of it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And this is a hard part of the story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. At a conference in Berlin in 1884 and 1885, the great powers recognize Leopold as the ruler of a vast territory in central Africa, about eighty times the size of Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was not a Belgian colony. It was the king's personal property, called the Congo Free State.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And what followed?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the worst atrocities of the colonial era.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Leopold's agents forced villagers to collect rubber and ivory, under a system of terror.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Hostages were taken, villages burned, and people who failed to meet quotas were beaten, mutilated, or killed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians estimate that millions of Congolese died from violence, starvation, and disease during these years, although the exact numbers are debated.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How did the world find out?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Reports by missionaries, journalists, and the British diplomat Roger Casement, and a campaign led by the journalist Edmund Morel, eventually produced an international outcry.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1908, under heavy pressure, the Belgian state took over the colony from the king, and it became the Belgian Congo, which Belgium ruled until 1960.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that money ended up in Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Partly. The money that Leopold drew from the Congo went partly into building, and into impressing.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He built the great Cinquantenaire park and its triumphal arch, to commemorate fifty years of Belgian independence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He built wide avenues, such as Avenue Louise, and monuments, and royal greenhouses at Laeken, and a huge museum of Central Africa in the suburb of Tervuren.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the world's fair.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the Brussels world's fair of 1897, he organized a colonial exhibition in which Congolese people were put on display in a replica village.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The grand showpiece of Belgium's capital had been paid for, in part, by a terrible human cost.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And that's a story Brussels has been grappling with ever since.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Meanwhile, something very different was happening in architecture.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the eighteen-nineties, a group of young architects, led by Victor Horta, create a new style that rejects the heavy historical imitations of the time.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They use iron, glass, and sweeping curves inspired by plants and flowers, in what comes to be known as Art Nouveau, or the new art.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Tassel house.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1893 and 1894, Horta builds a townhouse for a professor named Emile Tassel, in which iron columns shaped like stems, and stairs twining like vines, flow through the whole house, with light pouring in from above.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's widely regarded as the first Art Nouveau building.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Others followed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Paul Hankar and Henry van de Velde, among others.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The style spreads to Paris, Vienna, and Barcelona.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But it started in Brussels. Several of Horta's townhouses are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So by 1900, what kind of city is Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A prosperous, confident metropolis of more than half a million people in its wider urban area.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A city of cafés, department stores, glass-roofed shopping arcades, and boulevards.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a French-speaking city. At the time of independence, a large share of ordinary Brusselers spoke a Dutch dialect, but French was the language of government, business, education, and prestige.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And over the nineteenth century, it steadily took over.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And today it's officially bilingual.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the question of language, which was just beginning to stir in the late nineteenth century, will return again and again in the story of modern Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the fates of small countries rest on the decisions of large ones.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The guarantee of Belgian neutrality, signed in 1839, is now seventy-five years old.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in the summer of 1914, a crisis in the Balkans pushes Europe toward war.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Germany's plan to defeat France calls for an army to march through neutral Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: If someone wants to see this chapter in stone?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Walk the Boulevard Anspach and look at the grand facades of the Bourse.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Visit the Palace of Justice, whose terrace has a famous view over the whole city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And if you have time for one museum, make it the Horta Museum in Saint-Gilles, the house where the architect lived and worked.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Next, two wars, a world's fair with a giant atom, and a city that becomes the capital of Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A lot to cover. Let's go.
